passage: In the hostel common room, the tablet was allowed only on Saturdays. Kamal, nine, went to Rukmini Ma'am's desk at five. "Just five minutes, Ma'am? Only to finish one level." She nodded. At quarter past five he was back. "Ma'am, the level has a second part. Five more minutes?" She nodded again. At six: "Ma'am, can I play until dinner? It's almost dinner anyway." Then, after dinner, sweetly: "Ma'am, I've already played so long, the whole evening is almost gone. Can I just keep it till lights-out?" Rukmini Ma'am looked up from her register and laughed. "Kamal, you started with five minutes."

qa.a: She could ask herself whether she would have agreed if Kamal had first asked to play until dinner; if not, she can kindly say the tablet time is over.

qa.a: She seems amused as she notices how five minutes grew step by step, and perhaps a little caught out by how natural each yes had seemed.

passage: I'm Deepika, Farida's big sister, and I watched her do it again on Sunday. First she asked Ammi, "Can I watch just one cartoon?" Ammi said yes. When it ended, Farida said, "That one was short, can I watch the next one?" Yes again. Then, "Can I finish the season? Only a few are left." Ammi was cooking and said, "Hmm, okay." By the time the sun went down, Farida had watched the whole evening. Her homework was still in her bag. I don't think she planned it like a trick. Each step just seemed small after the one before. Ammi looked at the clock in surprise, as if she didn't know where the time had gone.

"No." "Then twenty minutes, and then cricket outside."

qa.a: "If you'd asked for the whole evening on Monday, what would I have said?" It made her judge Friday's request on its own, not as a small step after the others.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt when she stopped herself on Friday?
qa.a: She seems a little startled at how ten minutes had grown to a whole evening in five days, since each ask had felt so small, so she settles on twenty minutes and cricket.

passage: Abhinav, you think you invented 'just five more minutes'? Your Irfan Nana was a champion. When I was ten, in Lucknow, the neighbours had a carrom board and we didn't. One Sunday I asked my father, 'Abba, can I play just one game at Qureshi sahib's house?' One game, he said. Fine. After that, I came back. 'Abba, the game was very short. One more?' Fine. Then: 'Abba, they're starting a tournament. It'll finish before Maghrib.' 'Hmm, okay.' Then: 'Abba, it's the final! Can I stay till dinner? Qureshi aunty said I can eat there.' And he said yes, because every yes before it had made this one feel like the next step. I came home at nine, powder up to my elbows. My father looked at the clock and said, 'When did this become the whole day?' I didn't have an answer.

qa.q: Where did young Irfan go to play carrom?
qa.a: He went to Qureshi sahib's house, because the neighbours had a carrom board.

qa.q: Why did young Irfan keep asking for a little more?
qa.a: Each small yes made the next request feel like a natural next step, so he kept stretching one game into the whole day.

qa.q: What could Abhinav learn from Nana's story about asking for more time?
qa.a: Abhinav could notice when 'just five more minutes' keeps growing and ask himself what he really wants, instead of stretching each yes into the whole evening.

qa.q: How might Irfan's father have felt looking at the clock?
qa.a: His father was probably surprised and a bit annoyed, realising that his small yeses had added up to a whole day.

grounding: A grandfather tells his grandchild how, as a boy, one small yes to a carrom game led step by step to a whole day, each request feeling like a natural next step.

passage: The train to Chennai was delayed four hours, and the waiting room was hot and crowded. Francis, nine, tugged at his father's sleeve. 'Papa, can I play the car game on your phone? Just five minutes?' Samir was busy on a call with the railway helpline. He nodded. Five minutes later: 'Papa, I didn't finish the race. Five more?' Nod. Then: 'Papa, the train's so late. Can I play until the announcement?' Samir, now arguing with a ticket clerk, waved his hand. 'Okay, okay.' Then: 'Papa, since the train's still late, can I play all evening?' 'Fine, fine.' Francis played race after race. At eight o'clock Samir reached for his phone to call Francis's mother about the new time. The screen was black. Battery dead. Samir stared at it. Francis looked down at his shoes. 'You said yes each time,' he said quietly.

qa.a: The train to Chennai was delayed four hours, so the waiting room was hot and crowded.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he looked down at his shoes?
qa.a: He seemed guilty and embarrassed that his game had drained the phone, even though he felt each yes had allowed it.

qa.q: At which point could Francis have stopped the requests growing, and how?
qa.a: When the first five minutes ended, he could have stopped, or asked himself whether Papa would agree to a whole evening if he had asked that first.

qa.q: How might Samir feel when he finds the phone dead?
qa.a: Samir probably feels frustrated and worried, since he needs to call Francis's mother, and he may realise his distracted yeses added up.
